overview: Pallava rulers governed parts of southern India, leaving inscriptions from the fourth to ninth centuries. The atlas divides their history between “Pallavas” in 500 to 800 and “Pallava” in 800 to 1000. These consecutive labels share this card; the final mapped century extends beyond the dynasty’s main political supremacy, which ended around 900. Its broad outlines are approximate, not precise boundaries of control.

periods.title: Earlier Pallava rule
periods.summary: The map begins during a dynasty whose surviving inscriptions already reach back into earlier centuries.

periods.title: Temples cut into rock
periods.summary: Mahendravarman I’s Mandagapattu inscription celebrates a sanctuary made without conventional building materials.

periods.title: Monuments beside the sea
periods.summary: Mamallapuram’s Pallava architecture combines rock-cut monuments with temples assembled from stone.

periods.title: Village wealth and learning
periods.summary: Ninth-century royal grants connect cultivated land, local households and a seat of learning at Bahur.

periods.title: After Pallava supremacy
periods.summary: Chola conquest ended the main royal power around this transition; the later map interval is an overhang.

sections.title: A capital, a port and a world of stone

items.text: Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital, while Mamallapuram served as a port and a remarkable setting for royal monuments. Their surviving buildings and carvings make the dynasty visible through the work of designers and sculptors as well as through the names of kings.

At Mandagapattu, a cave-temple inscription from about 600 to 625 celebrates King Mahendravarman I, also called Vicitracitta. It proudly lists what the builders did without: bricks, wood, metal and mortar. Cutting the sanctuary into rock made the hillside itself the building material.

Mamallapuram’s rathas resemble miniature temple buildings, but each was carved from a large boulder. Their name evokes chariots; these stone monuments did not roll anywhere. Roof forms, columns and sculpted details show craftspeople exploring architecture while removing rock rather than stacking it.

The Shore Temple represents another approach: a structural temple assembled from masonry beside the sea. Together with the nearby caves and monolithic shrines, it lets visitors compare different solutions to the same challenge: making a durable sacred building from stone.

The Great Relief fills a rock face with gods, people and animals, including elephants with calves. Scholars debate whether its central story is the descent of the Ganges or Arjuna’s penance. One small scene is deliciously suspicious: a cat imitates an ascetic while mice gather nearby. A holy-looking cat is still a cat.

An eighth-century Pallava granite panel in the National Museum shows a divine family: Shiva, Parvati and their child Skanda, seated on his mother’s lap. Brahma and Vishnu appear behind them. Called Somaskanda, the image brings an intimate parent-and-child grouping into a grand religious setting.

sections.title: Water, food and the work of a village

items.text: The great well at Tiruvellarai had a named builder, Kampan Araiyan. Its inscription says construction began in Dantivarman’s fourth regnal year and finished in his fifth, around the turn of the ninth century. It also assigns responsibility for protecting the endowment. Providing water meant both construction and continuing local care.

A Kunnandarkoyil inscription records 200 nali of rice for feeding 100 people at the Tiruvadirai festival. The editor tentatively places it under ninth-century Nandivarman III. Someone had to plan the provisions for a substantial gathering: this inscription is almost a surviving festival shopping note.

The late-eighth-century Tandantottam charter permitted its privileged Brahmin grantees to build brick houses, dig wells and reservoirs, plant coconut groves and install large oil presses. This was a specific land grant with special rights, offering a close view of how homes, water and production were connected.

The same charter lists exemptions involving looms, oil presses, potters, shepherds, market stalls and marriage fees. A tax list may sound dull, but it preserves a bustling cast of workers and transactions. These exemptions belonged to the granted settlement, rather than to every family under Pallava rule.

The Tandantottam land allocations included two shares for a physician, along with support for water supply at a public hall and for water distribution. This is concrete evidence that medical work and water services could receive resources within a village endowment.

That charter also allotted a share to a reciter of the Bharata epic and another to a drummer. Stories and music had an economic place alongside water work and accounting. Learning could reach listeners through a performer’s voice.

At Uttiramerur, a record dated to Nandivarman’s twenty-fourth year describes Perumancikan buying three plots before donating them to a temple. One seller was a Brahmin woman, identified through her husband, Tatakkati of Irayur. Her share appears alongside those of male sellers, preserving a particular woman’s place in a land transaction.

Revenue from those Uttiramerur plots was assigned to rice-and-ghee offerings twice daily. The great assembly exempted the land from taxes. Religious routine depended on practical agreements about property, income and food, with the arrangements cut into stone so that later people could read them.

In the ninth century, Nripatungavarman’s Bahur charter assigned three villages to a seat of learning. Agricultural resources helped sustain its learned community. This was endowed scholarly education; the record does not describe a school attended by every child in the surrounding countryside.

The Bahur grant describes a lived landscape: house plots and houses, gardens, wet and dry fields, wells, tanks, storehouses and ground for grazing calves. These details bring the college’s support system down to earth, among households, crops, stored supplies and young cattle.

The copper charter even remembers the craftsman who made its writing. The goldsmith Nripatunga names his father, Matevi-peruntattan, and grandfather, Uditodaya-peruntattan, from a quarter of Kanchipuram. A royal document thus preserves a skilled family’s names as well as the king’s.

sections.title: Words that survive, and what happened next

items.text: Try one word from the Mandagapattu inscription: “aniṣṭakam”, meaning “without bricks”. This is the scholarly Roman transliteration of Sanskrit carved in Grantha script around 600 to 625. The word belongs to the king’s proud description of his rock-cut temple: a tiny sample of an original building announcement.

Chola records describe Aditya I defeating the Pallava ruler Aparajita and taking his country. Yet conquest did not erase every older obligation. At Tirukkalukkunram, an inscription in Aditya’s twenty-seventh year renewed a grant associated with earlier Pallava kings. A new ruler could preserve an old endowment.

ending.text: The main Pallava royal power ended with Chola conquest around 900. The atlas’s label continuing to 1000 should not imply another century of unchanged Pallava sovereignty. Earlier endowments could survive under new rulers, alongside the communities and monuments they supported.
